title: Daphne
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Apollo's first love, and the poem's first pursuit. Fresh from killing the serpent Python at Delphi, Apollo mocks Cupid for carrying a bow, and Cupid answers with two arrows — gold to make love, lead to refuse it — and puts one in each of them. Daphne, daughter of the Thessalian river-god Peneus, has already asked her father for lifelong virginity, as Diana was given it by hers; Apollo, struck with desire, pleads, boasts, and then runs her to exhaustion, and she escapes only by praying to the river-waters to destroy the shape that has drawn him. She becomes the laurel, and the god who could not have her claims the tree instead — the wreath of the Roman triumph, and the pair of laurels that stood at Augustus' door in Ovid's own city. The Latin is direct about the terror of the chase and about the god's persistence after the change, and nothing has been softened here in either direction.

advisory.lede: This part is an attempted rape: Apollo pursues Daphne, who escapes only by being turned into a laurel tree.
advisory.more: Ovid tells the pursuit at length and largely from Apollo's side; the narrative does not condemn him, and Daphne's escape costs her the body and the life she had. Lectorium presents the text as written, and the translation neither sharpens the Latin nor softens it. This is the first of the poem's rape narratives — Io, Callisto, Proserpina and Philomela follow.

sentences.t:
Primus amor Phoebi Daphne Peneia, quem non
fors ignara dedit, sed saeva Cupidinis ira.
sentences.l:
Phoebus' first love was Daphne, daughter of Peneus, which not
unknowing chance gave, but the savage wrath of Cupid.
sentences.i: Phoebus' first love was Daphne, the daughter of Peneus — a love no blind chance gave him, but the savage wrath of Cupid.
sentences.n: 'Peneia' is a patronymic adjective, 'daughter of Peneus', the river-god of Thessaly; the name comes back in three further forms — 'Peneide' (472), 'Penei' (504), 'Peneidas' (544) — and the notes flag each. 'ignara' is active in force — chance that does not know, blind. 'quem' picks up 'amor', so the love itself is what was given.

sentences.t:
Delius hunc, nuper victa serpente superbus,
viderat adducto flectentem cornua nervo
sentences.l:
The Delian had seen him — lately, with the serpent conquered, proud —
bending his bow-horns with the string drawn tight,
sentences.i: The Delian, still proud from his recent conquest of the serpent, had seen him bending his bow with the string drawn tight,
sentences.n: 'Delius' is Apollo, born on Delos; Ovid names gods by their cult-places constantly. 'nuper victa serpente' and 'adducto ... nervo' are both ablative absolutes — a self-contained 'with X done' where English wants a clause. 'cornua', 'horns', are the bow's two tips, and so the bow itself.

sentences.t:
“quid” que “tibi, lascive puer, cum fortibus armis?”
dixerat,
sentences.l:
and 'what have you, wanton boy, to do with brave weapons?'
he had said,
sentences.i: and 'what business have you, wanton boy, with the weapons of the brave?' he had said,
sentences.n: 'quid tibi cum ...?' is an idiom needing no verb: a dative of the person, then 'cum' with the ablative — 'what have you to do with ...?'. 'lascive' is 'playful, wanton' — the jibe of a grown man at a child at play, not an accusation of lust. The '-que' printed outside the quotation marks joins this sentence to 'viderat': it is the sentence's second word, and the sentence begins inside the speech.

sentences.t:
“ista decent umeros gestamina nostros,
qui dare certa ferae, dare vulnera possumus hosti,
sentences.l:
those trappings of yours befit our own shoulders,
who can give sure wounds to a wild beast, give them to an enemy,
sentences.i: gear like that befits shoulders such as mine — shoulders that can deal a beast its certain wound, or an enemy his.
sentences.n: 'nostros' and 'possumus' are the plural of majesty: Apollo speaks of himself as 'we'. 'certa ... vulnera' is one phrase split across the two 'dare's, so that a single gift is made to sound like two.

sentences.t:
qui modo pestifero tot iugera ventre prementem
stravimus innumeris tumidum Pythona sagittis.
sentences.l:
we who lately, with arrows past counting, laid low swollen Python
as he pressed so many acres beneath his plague-bearing belly.
sentences.i: we who not long ago brought down bloated Python with arrows past counting, where he lay crushing acre upon acre under his pestilent belly.
sentences.n: The Python was the serpent Apollo killed at Delphi, in the lines just before these. 'iugera' are Roman land-measures, so the monster is laid out and measured like a field. 'prementem' agrees with 'Pythona' but stands a whole line away from it — Ovid's habit of splitting a noun from what modifies it.

sentences.t:
Tu face nescio quos esto contentus amores
inritare tua, nec laudes adsere nostras.”
sentences.l:
You — be content to provoke with that torch of yours
some loves or other, and do not lay claim to praise that is ours.
sentences.i: You be content to kindle some passions or other with that torch of yours, and do not claim credit that belongs to me.
sentences.n: 'nescio quos' is a fixed dismissive idiom, 'some ... or other', said with contempt. 'esto' is the future imperative, stiffer and more magisterial than 'es'. Cupid's weapon here is the torch, not the bow: Apollo has just denied him arrows, and is about to be shot with one.

sentences.t:
Filius huic Veneris “figat tuus omnia, Phoebe,
te meus arcus:” ait
sentences.l:
The son of Venus to him: 'let your [bow] pierce all things, Phoebus —
you, my bow,' he said,
sentences.i: Venus' son answered him: 'Let your bow pierce all things, Phoebus; let mine pierce you,' he said,
sentences.n: 'figat' is a jussive subjunctive, a concession offered before the sting: 'let it pierce ...'. The second clause has no verb of its own — 'te meus arcus' borrows 'figat' — and 'te' stands first, where the blow lands. 'huic' is a dative waiting all the way to 'ait' for its verb of speaking.

sentences.t:
“quantoque animalia cedunt
cuncta deo tanto minor est tua gloria nostra.”
sentences.l:
and by as much as all living creatures yield
to a god, by so much is your glory less than ours.
sentences.i: and by as much as every living thing gives way before a god, by that much is your glory less than mine.
sentences.n: 'quanto ... tanto' is a proportional pair in the ablative of measure of difference: 'by however much ..., by that much ...'. 'nostra' is the plural of majesty again — Cupid answers Apollo in Apollo's own register.

sentences.t:
Dixit et eliso percussis aere pennis
inpiger umbrosa Parnasi constitit arce
sentences.l:
He spoke, and with the air driven out by the beat of his wings,
tireless, took his stand on the shadowy height of Parnassus,
sentences.i: He spoke, and, with the air driven out under the stroke of his wings, tireless, he came to rest on the shaded crag of Parnassus,
sentences.n: 'eliso ... aere percussis ... pennis' braids two ablatives together with the participles pulled away from their nouns: 'the air squeezed out, his wings having struck it'. 'inpiger' (the edition's spelling for 'impiger') is an adjective doing an adverb's work — 'tireless' where English wants 'tirelessly'.

sentences.t:
eque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra
diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem.
sentences.l:
and from his arrow-bearing quiver drew two shafts
of opposite work: this one drives love off, that one makes it.
sentences.n: 'eque' is 'e' + '-que', 'and out of'. 'diversorum operum' is a genitive of quality, 'of opposite working'. 'hoc' is the nearer of the two, 'illud' the further; Ovid then takes them up again in reverse order in the next two lines.

sentences.t:
Quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta;
quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum.
sentences.l:
The one that makes it is golden and glitters with a sharp point;
the one that drives it off is blunt and has lead beneath the reed.
sentences.n: A matched pair, clause for clause — 'quod facit' against 'quod fugat', gold against lead, point against blunt. 'harundine' is the reed shaft; a Roman arrow was reed with a metal head, so the two metals are the arrows' real material, not decoration.

sentences.t:
Hoc deus in nympha Peneide fixit, at illo
laesit Apollineas traiecta per ossa medullas.
sentences.l:
This one the god fixed in the nymph, daughter of Peneus; but with that one
he wounded Apollo's marrow through bones pierced clean through.
sentences.i: The lead one the god planted in Peneus' daughter; with the golden one he pierced the bones through and wounded Apollo's own marrow.
sentences.n: 'hoc' is the lead shaft just described, 'illo' the gold: Daphne gets the arrow that repels, Apollo the one that inflames. 'traiecta per ossa' is a participle where English wants a clause, 'the bones pierced through'. Ovid names the victim by adjective — 'Apollineas ... medullas', 'Apollo's marrow' — rather than by pronoun. 'Peneide' is the same patronymic as 'Peneia' in 452, here in a Greek-declined ablative.

sentences.t:
Protinus alter amat, fugit altera nomen amantis
silvarum tenebris captivarumque ferarum
exuviis gaudens innuptaeque aemula Phoebes.
sentences.l:
At once the one loves, the other flees the very name of a lover,
taking joy in the woods' darkness and in the spoils
of beasts she has taken, a rival of unwedded Phoebe.
sentences.i: At once he is in love; she flees the very word 'lover', delighting in the shadows of the forest and the pelts of the game she takes — a rival of Phoebe, who never married.
sentences.n: 'alter ... altera' sets the two apart by gender alone: he, she. She flees not the lover but 'nomen amantis', the name of one — the whole category. 'Phoebe' is Diana, Apollo's own twin, so Daphne's model is the pursuer's sister.

sentences.t: Vitta coercebat positos sine lege capillos.
sentences.l: A headband was confining her hair, laid without law.
sentences.i: A single band confined her hair, which lay where it would.
sentences.n: 'positos sine lege' — 'placed without rule': the hair is unarranged, and the phrase carries the whole characterisation. 'coercebat' is imperfect, a standing state rather than an act. Ovid will undo this line at 529, when the wind takes the same hair as she runs.

sentences.t:
Multi illam petiere, illa aversata petentes
inpatiens expersque viri nemora avia lustrat,
nec quid Hymen, quid Amor, quid sint conubia curat.
sentences.l:
Many sought her; she, turning away from those who sought,
impatient of a man and untouched by one, ranges the pathless groves,
nor cares what Hymen, what Love, what wedlock may be.
sentences.i: Many courted her; she turned from her suitors and, wanting no man and knowing none, ranged the trackless woods, caring nothing for what Hymen, or Love, or marriage might be.
sentences.n: 'petiere' is 'petierunt', the poetic third-plural perfect in '-ere'; it is everywhere in Ovid and means exactly what the longer form means. 'expers viri' is 'having no share of a man', a genitive of the thing lacked. 'quid sint conubia' is an indirect question, hence the subjunctive 'sint'. Hymen is the god of the wedding itself, called by name in the marriage-song.

sentences.t:
Saepe pater dixit “generum mihi, filia, debes,”
saepe pater dixit “debes mihi nata, nepotes:”
sentences.l:
Often her father said, 'you owe me a son-in-law, daughter';
often her father said, 'you owe me grandsons, child.'
sentences.n: The repetition is the point: the same three words open both lines, and only the demand changes — first a son-in-law, then grandsons. 'debes' with an accusative of the thing owed makes the daughter the family's debtor. 'nata', 'born one', is an ordinary tender word for daughter.

sentences.t:
illa, velut crimen taedas exosa iugales,
pulchra verecundo suffunditur ora rubore,
sentences.l:
she, hating the wedding torches as though they were a crime,
is flooded, as to her lovely face, with a modest blush.
sentences.i: she, loathing the wedding torches as if they were a crime, is flooded across her lovely face with a modest red.
sentences.n: 'ora' is the Greek accusative of respect after the passive 'suffunditur' — she is suffused *as to* her face. Ovid uses this Greek turn constantly for parts of the body, and English has to convert it into 'her face flushed'. 'taedas ... iugales' are the pine torches carried in the wedding procession, standing here for marriage itself.

sentences.t:
inque patris blandis haerens cervice lacertis
“da mihi perpetua, genitor carissime,” dixit
“virginitate frui: dedit hoc pater ante Dianae.”
sentences.l:
and clinging to her father's neck with coaxing arms,
'grant me, dearest begetter,' she said,
'to have the use of virginity for ever: a father gave this before to Diana.'
sentences.i: and clinging to her father's neck with wheedling arms she said, 'Dearest father, grant that I may keep my maidenhood for ever: Diana's father granted her that before me.'
sentences.n: 'frui' takes the ablative, so 'perpetua ... virginitate' is the thing enjoyed — and adjective and noun stand at opposite ends of the request, with the whole of it between them. 'blandis ... lacertis' is an ablative of means, and 'blandis' judges the gesture: coaxing. Diana had asked her father Jupiter for perpetual virginity and been given it; Daphne is asking for a precedent already set.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem obsequitur, sed te decor iste quod optas
esse vetat.
sentences.l:
He indeed gives way; but that beauty of yours forbids you
to be what you pray for.
sentences.n: Ovid turns and speaks to Daphne herself: 'te ... optas'. This is apostrophe, the poet stepping out of the narrative to address a character, and he keeps it up through the next line. 'vetat' governs the infinitive 'esse', with 'quod optas' as its complement.

sentences.t:
Votoque tuo tua forma repugnat:
Phoebus amat visaeque cupit conubia Daphnes,
quodque cupit, sperat, suaque illum oracula fallunt.
sentences.l:
and your own beauty fights your own prayer.
Phoebus loves, and desires marriage with Daphne, once seen,
and what he desires he hopes for, and his own oracles deceive him.
sentences.i: and your own beauty fights against your own prayer. Phoebus loves; he has seen Daphne and wants her in marriage; what he wants, he expects — and his own oracles fail him.
sentences.n: 'visae ... Daphnes' is a Greek genitive ('Daphnes', not 'Daphnae') with a participle folded inside it: 'of Daphne, seen'. The last clause is the hinge of the whole scene — the god of prophecy cannot read his own future. 'fallunt' is 'deceive': not that the oracles are false, but that they do not serve their owner.

sentences.t:
Utque leves stipulae demptis adolentur aristis,
ut facibus saepes ardent, quas forte viator
vel nimis admovit vel iam sub luce reliquit,
sentences.l:
And as light stubble burns once the ears are taken off,
as hedges burn from torches which a traveller by chance
has brought too near, or has left behind now under the light,
sentences.i: And as the light stubble goes up once the ears of grain are cut, as a hedge takes fire from a torch that some traveller has brought too close, or left lying at first light —
sentences.n: 'demptis ... aristis' is an ablative absolute: the field burns only after the harvest is off it. 'adolentur' is passive with no agent named, so the stubble seems simply to catch of itself. 'sub luce' is 'at the coming of light', dawn, when the traveller no longer needs his torch and drops it still alight.

sentences.t:
sic deus in flammas abiit, sic pectore toto
uritur et sterilem sperando nutrit amorem.
sentences.l:
so the god went off into flame, so with his whole breast
he burns, and feeds a barren love by hoping.
sentences.i: so the god went up in flame; so he burns through the whole of his breast and nurses a fruitless love on hope.
sentences.n: 'in flammas abiit' is literally 'went away into flames', the idiom for being consumed. 'sperando' is a gerund in the ablative, 'by hoping' — hope is what keeps the love alive, and 'sterilem' says in advance that it will bear nothing.

sentences.t:
Spectat inornatos collo pendere capillos
et “quid, si comantur?” ait. Videt igne micantes
sideribus similes oculos, videt oscula, quae non
est vidisse satis;
sentences.l:
He watches her unadorned hair hang at her neck
and says, 'what if it were dressed?' He sees her eyes flashing with fire,
like stars; he sees her lips, which it is not
enough to have seen;
sentences.i: He gazes at her unadorned hair falling at her neck and says, 'and what if it were done up?' He sees her eyes flashing with fire, like stars; he sees her lips — and to have seen them is not enough.
sentences.n: 'spectat ... pendere' is accusative and infinitive after a verb of seeing: 'he watches the hair hang'. 'comantur' is a present subjunctive in a supposition, 'suppose it were arranged'. 'oscula' means lips and kisses at once, and the ambiguity is the point: the clause 'quae non est vidisse satis' is where looking turns into wanting.

sentences.t:
laudat digitosque manusque
bracchiaque et nudos media plus parte lacertos.
sentences.l:
he praises her fingers and her hands
and her forearms and her upper arms, bare more than halfway.
sentences.n: The piled '-que ... -que ... -que' is a verse mannerism that lets the list run on without stopping, as the eye runs. Latin distinguishes 'bracchia', the forearm, from 'lacerti', the upper arm; 'media plus parte', 'more than the middle part', measures exactly how much of her the god can see.

sentences.t:
Siqua latent, meliora putat. Fugit ocior aura
illa levi neque ad haec revocantis verba resistit:
sentences.l:
If anything is hidden, he thinks it better still. She flees, swifter
than a light breeze, and does not halt at these words of his calling her back:
sentences.i: Whatever is hidden he takes to be better still. But she is in flight, swifter than a light breeze, and does not stop for the words he calls after her:
sentences.n: 'ocior aura ... levi' is a comparative with the ablative of comparison, adjective and noun split across the line-break so that her speed and its measure sit at opposite ends. 'revocantis' is a participle used as a noun in the genitive, 'of the one calling her back'. This is the line where the cataloguing look becomes a pursuit.

sentences.t: “Nympha, precor, Penei, mane! Non insequor hostis:
sentences.l: 'Nymph, I beg you, daughter of Peneus, stay! I do not follow as an enemy:
sentences.n: 'Penei' is the vocative of the patronymic — 'you, daughter of Peneus' (compare 'Peneia' at 452). 'hostis' is nominative, not the object: 'I do not pursue *as* an enemy'. The word means a public enemy in war, and it is the comparison he chooses to deny.

sentences.t:
nympha, mane! sic agna lupum, sic cerva leonem,
sic aquilam penna fugiunt trepidante columbae,
hostes quaeque suos: amor est mihi causa sequendi.
sentences.l:
nymph, stay! It is so that the lamb flees the wolf, so the hind the lion,
so, on trembling wing, the doves flee the eagle —
each its own enemies: love is my reason for following.
sentences.i: Nymph, stay! This is how the lamb runs from the wolf, the hind from the lion, the dove on a shaking wing from the eagle — each from its own enemy. Love is my reason for following.
sentences.n: Apollo names three pairs of hunter and prey in order to say that he is not one of them — every pair he picks is a killing pair. 'penna ... trepidante' is an ablative of manner, 'on a trembling wing', split around 'fugiunt'. 'quaeque' is 'each one', gathering all three fleeing females; 'sequendi' is a gerund in the genitive, 'of following'.

sentences.t:
Me miserum! ne prona cadas indignave laedi
crura notent sentes et sim tibi causa doloris.
sentences.l:
Wretched me! — do not fall headlong, and let no brambles mark
your legs, undeserving to be hurt, and let me not be a cause of pain to you.
sentences.i: Ah, wretched me! Do not fall on your face; let no briars scratch legs that deserve no hurt; let me not be the cause of your pain.
sentences.n: 'Me miserum' is an accusative of exclamation, a set cry. The three clauses 'ne ... -ve ... et' are negative wishes with the subjunctive — 'cadas', 'notent', 'sim'. 'indigna laedi' takes a passive infinitive after the adjective, a Greek turn: 'not deserving to be hurt'. He pities her legs while chasing her.

sentences.t:
Aspera, qua properas, loca sunt. Moderatius, oro,
curre fugamque inhibe; moderatius insequar ipse.
sentences.l:
Rough, where you are hurrying, the ground is. More gently, I beg,
run, and rein in your flight; more gently I will follow myself.
sentences.i: The ground where you are running is rough. Run more slowly, I beg you, and check your flight; I will follow more slowly myself.
sentences.n: 'qua' is 'by which way, where', and its clause is dropped inside the main one, splitting 'Aspera' from 'loca'. 'moderatius' is a comparative adverb, said twice: the bargain he offers is about speed, not about stopping.

sentences.t:
Cui placeas, inquire tamen. Non incola montis,
non ego sum pastor, non hic armenta gregesque
horridus observo.
sentences.l:
Ask, though, whom you are pleasing. I am no mountain-dweller,
I am no shepherd, I do not, all shaggy, keep watch here
over cattle and flocks.
sentences.i: Ask all the same whose fancy you have taken. I am no mountain man, no shepherd; I am not some unkempt fellow watching cattle and sheep out here.
sentences.n: 'Cui placeas' is an indirect question — 'whom you are pleasing' — hence the subjunctive, with the dative 'cui' governed by 'placeas'. 'horridus' is nominative and describes the imagined herdsman: rough, bristling, unwashed. The argument he makes is one of rank, not of safety.

sentences.t:
Nescis, temeraria, nescis
quem fugias, ideoque fugis.
sentences.l:
You do not know, rash girl, you do not know
whom you are fleeing, and that is why you flee.
sentences.n: The repeated 'nescis' brackets the vocative — the pause of a man losing patience. 'quem fugias' is another indirect question with the subjunctive. 'ideoque fugis' turns her refusal into ignorance: on his account she runs only because she does not know who he is.

sentences.t:
Mihi Delphica tellus
et Claros et Tenedos Patareaque regia servit,
Iuppiter est genitor; per me quod eritque fuitque
estque patet; per me concordant carmina nervis.
sentences.l:
The Delphic land serves me,
and Claros and Tenedos and the royal house of Patara;
Jupiter is my father; through me what will be and has been
and is lies open; through me songs are matched to strings.
sentences.i: The land of Delphi serves me, and Claros, and Tenedos, and the royal seat of Patara; Jupiter is my father. Through me, what will be and what has been and what is stands open; through me song and string keep time together.
sentences.n: Four places of Apollo's cult; Delphi, Claros and Patara were seats of his oracle. 'quod eritque fuitque estque' lines up three tenses of one verb and hangs them from a single 'quod' — the whole of time as one object of knowledge. 'servit' is singular with a compound subject, normal in verse. 'concordant carmina nervis' takes the dative after a verb of agreeing.

sentences.t:
Certa quidem nostra est, nostra tamen una sagitta
certior, in vacuo quae vulnera pectore fecit.
sentences.l:
Sure indeed is our arrow — yet one arrow is surer
than ours, which made these wounds in a breast that was empty.
sentences.i: My arrow strikes true, indeed; yet one arrow strikes truer than mine — the one that made these wounds in a breast that till then was heart-free.
sentences.n: 'nostra ... nostra' repeated across the middle of the line, then 'certa ... certior': his own boast is turned into the measure of his defeat. 'in vacuo ... pectore' — the breast was empty, heart-whole, before Cupid's shot.

sentences.t:
Inventum medicina meum est, opiferque per orbem
dicor, et herbarum subiecta potentia nobis:
sentences.l:
Medicine is my invention, and through the world
I am called the help-bringer, and the power of herbs is put under us.
sentences.i: Medicine is my discovery; the world calls me the bringer of help; the power of herbs is under my hand.
sentences.n: 'inventum ... meum' is a noun, 'a thing found by me', with 'medicina' as its subject: medicine is my discovery. Apollo is the god of healing and the father of Asclepius — and the boast is set up here only to be knocked down two lines later.

sentences.t:
ei mihi, quod nullis amor est sanabilis herbis
nec prosunt domino, quae prosunt omnibus, artes.”
sentences.l:
alas for me, that love is curable by no herbs,
and that the arts which help everyone do not help their master.
sentences.n: 'ei mihi' is the standard cry of grief, with the dative. 'nullis ... herbis' is an ablative of means with the verbal adjective 'sanabilis', 'curable'. 'domino' and 'omnibus' are both datives with 'prosunt', and the relative clause is dropped inside the main one so that the master and everyone else stand side by side.

sentences.t:
Plura locuturum timido Peneia cursu
fugit cumque ipso verba inperfecta reliquit,
sentences.l:
Him, about to say more, Peneus' daughter fled with frightened running,
and left, along with the man himself, his words unfinished,
sentences.i: He would have said more, but Peneus' daughter fled him in terror and left his words unfinished along with the man who spoke them,
sentences.n: 'locuturum' is a future participle in the accusative, object of 'fugit': 'him, on the point of saying more'. 'cum ipso' is bleak wit — she abandons the sentence and the speaker in the same movement. 'timido ... cursu' is an ablative of manner, the adjective again doing an adverb's work.

sentences.t: tum quoque visa decens. Nudabant corpora venti,
sentences.l: then too she seemed comely. The winds were laying her body bare,
sentences.i: even then she seemed lovely. The winds kept stripping her body bare;
sentences.n: 'visa decens', 'she seemed comely', tells the reader whose eye is in use: the god's, not the narrator's alone. 'Nudabant' is the first of three imperfects in a row that hold the moment open while she runs.

sentences.t:
obviaque adversas vibrabant flamina vestes,
et levis inpulsos retro dabat aura capillos,
sentences.l:
and the gusts that met her set her clothes shaking against her,
and a light breeze was driving her hair back behind her,
sentences.i: the gusts that met her kept shaking her clothes against her, and a light breeze kept driving her hair back behind her,
sentences.n: 'obvia' and 'adversas' both mean 'facing, meeting head-on', doubled once for the wind and once for the clothes. Two more imperfects, 'vibrabant' and 'dabat'. The breeze undoes line 477: the hair that lay 'without law' under its headband is now taken by the wind.

sentences.t:
auctaque forma fuga est. Sed enim non sustinet ultra
perdere blanditias iuvenis deus,
sentences.l:
and her beauty was increased by flight. But the young god does not bear
to waste his coaxing words any longer,
sentences.i: and flight made her lovelier. But the young god will not go on spending sweet words for nothing,
sentences.n: 'sed enim' is an abrupt idiom, 'but the fact is'. 'perdere blanditias' is 'to waste flatteries' — the courtship was an outlay, and he stops paying it. This half-line is where persuasion ends and the chase proper begins.

sentences.t:
utque monebat
ipse Amor, admisso sequitur vestigia passu.
sentences.l:
and, as Love himself was urging him,
he follows her footsteps at a loosed pace.
sentences.i: and, with Love himself urging him on, he runs down her tracks at full stride.
sentences.n: 'admisso ... passu' is an ablative absolute borrowed from horsemanship — 'with the pace let go', said of giving a horse its head. Ovid keeps 'ipse Amor' as the one giving the orders: the god who mocked Cupid is now taking instructions from him.

sentences.t:
Ut canis in vacuo leporem cum Gallicus arvo
vidit, et hic praedam pedibus petit, ille salutem:
sentences.l:
As when a Gallic hound has sighted a hare in an open field,
and the one makes for its prey with its feet, the other for safety:
sentences.i: As when a Gallic hound has sighted a hare in open ground, and the one runs for its prey and the other for its life —
sentences.n: 'cum' is postponed, standing late in its own clause after 'ut canis in vacuo leporem'; read it as 'ut cum canis Gallicus ...'. The Gallic hound was the fast sight-hound of Roman coursing. 'hic' is the hound and 'ille' the hare, and 'praedam' against 'salutem' says what each of them is running for.

sentences.t:
alter inhaesuro similis iam iamque tenere
sperat et extento stringit vestigia rostro,
sentences.l:
the one, like one about to fasten on, hopes now, now
to hold it, and grazes its tracks with muzzle stretched out,
sentences.i: the one, like a creature already fastening on, hopes at every instant to have it, and skims its tracks with muzzle stretched out;
sentences.n: 'inhaesuro similis' — 'like one about to cling', a future participle in the dative after 'similis'; the hound is compared to one already fastening on, not said to be. 'iam iamque' is 'now, at any instant', the doubling doing the work of the near miss. 'stringit vestigia': the muzzle is so close that it brushes the ground the hare's feet have just left.

sentences.t:
alter in ambiguo est, an sit conprensus, et ipsis
morsibus eripitur tangentiaque ora relinquit:
sentences.l:
the other is in doubt whether it has been caught, and from the very
bites is torn free, and leaves the touching jaws behind:
sentences.i: the other is in doubt whether it is taken, and pulls free of the very teeth, and leaves behind the jaws that touched it:
sentences.n: 'in ambiguo est an ...' is 'is in doubt whether', with the subjunctive 'sit conprensus' ('conprensus' is the edition's spelling for 'comprensus'). 'eripitur' is passive in form with a middle force: it snatches itself away. 'tangentia ... ora' are jaws that are touching it and have not yet closed.

sentences.t: sic deus et virgo est hic spe celer, illa timore.
sentences.l: so are the god and the maiden: he swift with hope, she with fear.
sentences.n: The whole simile closes on a single line and on two ablatives of cause, 'spe' and 'timore'. 'est' is singular although the subject is double, drawn to the nearer noun. The line tells the reader exactly what the hound and the hare were for.

sentences.t:
Qui tamen insequitur pennis adiutus Amoris,
ocior est requiemque negat tergoque fugacis
inminet et crinem sparsum cervicibus adflat.
sentences.l:
He, though, who pursues, helped by Love's wings,
is the swifter, and refuses her rest, and hangs over the back
of the fleeing girl, and breathes on the hair scattered at her neck.
sentences.i: But he who pursues, helped on by Love's wings, is the swifter; he grants her no rest; he looms at the fleeing girl's back and breathes on the hair spread across her neck.
sentences.n: 'Qui' opens the sentence — a connecting relative, 'and he'. 'fugacis' is an adjective used as a noun in the genitive, 'of the fleeing one'. 'inminet' takes the dative 'tergo', 'hangs over her back'. The last clause measures the distance in breath: not 'touches' but 'adflat', breathes upon.

sentences.t:
Viribus absumptis expalluit illa citaeque
victa labore fugae spectans Peneidas undas
sentences.l:
Her strength used up, she went white, and, beaten
by the labour of her swift flight, looking at the waters of Peneus,
sentences.i: Her strength spent, she went white and, beaten by the labour of her headlong flight, looking at the waters of Peneus
sentences.n: 'viribus absumptis' is an ablative absolute again — 'with her strength used up'. 'Peneidas' is a Greek accusative plural of the patronymic adjective, 'the Peneian waters': the river she turns to is her own father. Third form of the name, after 'Peneia' (452) and 'Penei' (504).

sentences.t: “fer pater” inquit “opem si flumina numen habetis.
sentences.l: 'bring help, father,' she said, 'if you rivers have divinity.
sentences.i: 'Father, bring help,' she said, 'if you rivers have any divine power;
sentences.n: 'fer' is the bare irregular imperative of 'fero'. 'flumina' is a vocative — she addresses the rivers as a class, her father among them, and 'habetis' is second plural to match. The 'si' clause is not doubt but the formula of prayer: if the power is yours, use it.

sentences.t:
qua nimium placui, tellus aut hisce vel istam,
Qua nimium placui, mutando perde figuram!”
sentences.l:
by which I have pleased too much — earth, either gape open, or that shape,
by which I have pleased too much, destroy it by changing it!'
sentences.i: '— by which I have pleased too well: earth, gape open, or else this shape of mine, by which I have pleased too well, destroy it by changing it!'
sentences.n: A genuine textual tangle: the edition prints the clause 'qua nimium placui', 'by which I have pleased too much', twice, once at the head of each line — and the first of the two has no antecedent until 'figuram' arrives in the second. The second witness prints instead 'mutando perde figuram quae facit ut laedar' — 'destroy by changing the shape that makes me suffer harm' — with no doubling and no appeal to the earth. Either way the prayer is the same: she asks to be destroyed as what she is. 'hisce' is the imperative of 'hisco', to gape open; 'mutando' is an ablative gerund, 'by changing'.

sentences.t:
Vix prece finita torpor gravis occupat artus:
mollia cinguntur tenui praecordia libro,
in frondem crines, in ramos bracchia crescunt,
sentences.l:
Her prayer scarcely finished, a heavy numbness takes her limbs:
her soft breast is bound about with thin bark,
her hair grows into leaves, her arms into branches,
sentences.i: Her prayer is barely done and a heavy numbness takes her limbs: thin bark closes round her soft breast, her hair grows into leaves, her arms into branches;
sentences.n: 'vix prece finita' is an ablative absolute doing the work of a time clause. From here the verbs go present and stay there — the change is shown happening rather than reported. 'praecordia' is the whole region in front of the heart, chest and midriff together.

sentences.t:
pes modo tam velox pigris radicibus haeret,
ora cacumen habet; remanet nitor unus in illa.
sentences.l:
the foot just now so swift clings fast in sluggish roots,
a treetop holds her face; one thing alone stays in her: her shining.
sentences.i: the foot that was so swift a moment ago is held fast in slow roots; a treetop takes her face; her brightness alone remains in her.
sentences.n: 'modo tam velox' — 'so swift only just now' — compresses the whole chase into three words, and 'pigris', 'sluggish', is set against it. 'ora cacumen habet' reverses the grammar one expects: the treetop is the subject and holds her face, not the other way about. 'nitor unus' is what the laurel keeps of her — the gloss of the leaf.

sentences.t:
Hanc quoque Phoebus amat, positaque in stipite dextra
sentit adhuc trepidare novo sub cortice pectus
sentences.l:
Her too Phoebus loves, and with his right hand set on the trunk
he feels her breast still trembling beneath the new bark,
sentences.i: Her too Phoebus loves, and laying his right hand on the trunk he feels her breast still shuddering under the new bark,
sentences.n: 'Hanc quoque' is 'her too', that is, the tree as well: the object has changed species and the desire has not. 'posita ... dextra' is another ablative absolute. 'sentit ... trepidare' is accusative and infinitive after a verb of perceiving, and 'adhuc', 'still, even now', is the hardest word in the line.

sentences.t:
conplexusque suis ramos, ut membra, lacertis
oscula dat ligno: refugit tamen oscula lignum.
sentences.l:
and having taken the branches in his arms, as though they were limbs,
he gives kisses to the wood: yet the wood shrinks back from his kisses.
sentences.i: and folding the branches in his arms as though they were limbs, he kisses the wood — and still the wood flinches from his kisses.
sentences.n: 'conplexus' (the edition's spelling for 'complexus') is a deponent participle, active in sense: 'having embraced'. In 'oscula dat ligno' the wood is a dative, the thing done to; in 'refugit ... oscula lignum' the same wood is the nominative subject and the kisses are what it flees. She has no voice left, and this is the only answer available to her.

sentences.t:
Cui deus “at quoniam coniunx mea non potes esse,
arbor eris certe” dixit “mea.
sentences.l:
And to her the god: 'but since you cannot be my wife,
a tree you shall certainly be,' he said, 'mine.
sentences.i: And the god said to her: 'But since you cannot be my wife, a tree you shall certainly be — and mine.
sentences.n: 'Cui' is a connecting relative, 'and to her'. 'quoniam' gives the reason and takes the indicative 'potes'. The possessive 'mea' is held back past 'dixit' into the following line, so the sentence lands on the word 'mine': the claim outlives the failure to take her.

sentences.t:
Semper habebunt
te coma, te citharae, te nostrae, laure, pharetrae:
sentences.l:
Always shall my hair have you,
you my lyres, you, laurel, my quivers:
sentences.i: You my hair shall have always, laurel, and you my lyre, and you my quiver:
sentences.n: The triple 'te ... te ... te' at the head of each clause, all on one verb, is the shape of a hymn — and he is making her one of his own attributes. 'laure' is the vocative: the first time she is addressed by her new name, and the name is a plant. 'citharae' and 'pharetrae' are plural for a single lyre and quiver, a habit of verse.

sentences.t:
tu ducibus Latiis aderis, cum laeta triumphum
vox canet et visent longas Capitolia pompas:
sentences.l:
you shall stand by Latin commanders, when the glad voice
sings the triumph and the Capitol looks on the long processions:
sentences.i: you shall attend the generals of Latium, when the glad shout hails the triumph and the Capitol looks out on the long processions;
sentences.n: 'aderis' takes the dative 'ducibus'. The triumph was the Roman victory procession up to the Capitol, with laurel worn by the general and carried by the troops; Ovid runs the myth forward into his own city. 'Capitolia' is neuter plural for the one hill, verse's habit again.

sentences.t:
postibus Augustis eadem fidissima custos
ante fores stabis mediamque tuebere quercum,
sentences.l:
at the doorposts of Augustus you, the same one, most faithful warden,
shall stand before the doors and guard the oak between them,
sentences.i: and you, the same tree, shall stand before the doors of Augustus, most faithful of guards, keeping watch over the oak in the middle,
sentences.n: Two laurels were set at the door of Augustus' house on the Palatine, with the civic oak-crown hung between them; Ovid's laurel is that laurel, and the myth is being made to end at an address in his own Rome. 'tuebere' is 'tueberis', the alternative second-singular future in '-re', common in verse. 'eadem', 'the same one', is still Daphne.

sentences.t:
utque meum intonsis caput est iuvenale capillis,
tu quoque perpetuos semper gere frondis honores.”
sentences.l:
and as my head is young with unshorn hair,
you too wear always the unending glory of your leaves.'
sentences.n: 'intonsis ... capillis' is an ablative of description; Apollo is the god who never cuts his hair, so the evergreen leaf is made to match him. 'gere' is imperative. 'perpetuos ... honores' answers Daphne's own 'perpetua ... virginitate' at 486 — she asked to keep one thing for ever, and this is the thing she is given to keep.

sentences.t:
Finierat Paean: factis modo laurea ramis
adnuit utque caput visa est agitasse cacumen.
sentences.l:
Paean had finished: the laurel, with branches only just made,
nodded assent, and seemed to have shaken its treetop as a head.
sentences.i: Paean had done: the laurel nodded with branches only a moment old, and seemed to have moved its top as one moves a head.
sentences.n: 'Paean' is Apollo under his healer's title, the name of the cry raised to him. 'factis modo ... ramis' is an ablative absolute — the branches were made a moment ago. 'adnuit' is the formal word for giving assent by a nod; 'visa est', 'she seemed', keeps the gesture at the level of appearance, and the Latin claims nothing beyond that.
